```{r setup}
library(vaster)
```

## Overview

vaster is deliberately small: a grid is a `dimension` and an `extent`, and every
operation is arithmetic on those six numbers. Many other tools carry the same
grid logic bundled with data, formats, or a CRS. This vignette lines vaster up
against a few of them, so you can see which vaster function stands in for a
concept you may already know.

The comparison chunks that call external packages (odc.geo, rasterio, magick,
reproj) are shown but not run here; the vaster chunks run.

## GDAL, terra, stars

GDAL represents a grid with a 6-element geotransform; terra and stars wrap that.
vaster converts to and from the same representation without an object or a file.
The [GDAL interoperability](gdal-interop.html) vignette covers this in full;
briefly:

```{r}
dimension <- c(360, 180)
extent <- c(-180, 180, -90, 90)

geo_transform0(dimension, extent)
```

A terra `SpatRaster` or stars object carries exactly this `dimension`/`extent`
(plus a CRS and, usually, data). When you only need the grid arithmetic -
cell indices, crop windows, coordinates - vaster does it without constructing
one.

## odc.geo GeoBox

[odc.geo](https://odc-geo.readthedocs.io/)'s `GeoBox` is a grid specification:
a shape (dimension), an affine transform (extent + resolution), and a CRS.
vaster is the first two of those - it holds no CRS. For the geometry, vaster's
`vaster_boundary()` reproduces `GeoBox.boundary()`: a coordinate for every cell
corner around the perimeter, which is what you densify before reprojecting so
the warped outline stays faithful.

```{r geobox, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.2, fig.alt = "The perimeter coordinates of an 8x5 grid, one point at every cell corner around the edge."}
dimension <- c(8, 5)
extent <- c(-2e6, 2.25e6, -5e6, -1e6)

b <- vaster_boundary(dimension, extent)
head(b)

op <- par(mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1), mgp = c(1.8, 0.6, 0))
plot(b, type = "o", pch = 19, cex = 0.6, asp = 1,
     col = "#1C6E8C", xlab = "x", ylab = "y")
par(op)
```

The equivalent in odc.geo, and the reprojection that motivates the densified
boundary, would be:

```{python, eval = FALSE}
from odc.geo.geobox import GeoBox
g = GeoBox.from_bbox((-2_000_000, -5_000_000, 2_250_000, -1_000_000),
                     "epsg:3577", resolution=1000)
g.boundary(100)   # perimeter points, like vaster_boundary()
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## vaster boundary -> lon/lat with reproj (reproj is not a vaster dependency)
lonlat <- reproj::reproj_xy(vaster_boundary(dimension, extent),
                            "OGC:CRS84", source = "EPSG:3577")
plot(lonlat, type = "l")
```

`vaster_boundary_cell()` gives the same traversal as cell indices, handy for
pulling boundary values out of a coordinate array.

## Rasterizing points to a grid

A common rasterio recipe turns scattered points into a count (or value) grid by
mapping each point to a pixel and accumulating. In vaster that is
`cell_from_xy()` to get the cell, then `tabulate()` to count - no raster object
and no I/O:

```{r rasterize, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "A coarse global count grid shaded from light to dark where more of the overlaid points fall."}
set.seed(3162)
pts <- cbind(x = rnorm(3000, 30, 60), y = rnorm(3000, -10, 35))

dimension <- c(72, 36)
extent <- c(-180, 180, -90, 90)

cell <- cell_from_xy(dimension, extent, pts)
counts <- tabulate(cell, nbins = n_cell(dimension))

## arrange cell-order counts into image() form (vaster_listxyz handles orientation)
m <- matrix(counts, nrow = dimension[2], ncol = dimension[1], byrow = TRUE)
xyz <- vaster_listxyz(dimension, extent, m)

op <- par(mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1), mgp = c(1.8, 0.6, 0))
image(xyz, col = hcl.colors(24, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE), asp = 1,
      xlab = "x", ylab = "y")
points(pts, pch = ".", col = "#00000055")
par(op)
```

The rasterio version builds an affine transform and calls `rowcol()` per point;
the grid logic is identical. Use `vaster_listxyz(..., corner = TRUE)` if you want
cell boundaries rather than centres for the `x`/`y` vectors.

## magick (pixel-space crops)

ImageMagick addresses an image as a pixel grid with a top-left origin and a
geometry string `WIDTHxHEIGHT+XOFF+YOFF` - the same convention as GDAL RasterIO.
`magick_geometry()` formats a crop extent into that string:

```{r}
magick_geometry(c(360, 180), c(-180, 180, -90, 90), c(110, 155, -45, -10))
```

which you can hand straight to magick:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(magick)
img <- image_read("world.png")
image_crop(img, magick_geometry(c(360, 180), c(-180, 180, -90, 90),
                                c(110, 155, -45, -10)))
```

It is the pixel-space sibling of `rasterio0()` / `rasterio_to_sfio()`; only the
output format differs.

## Summary

| Other tool | Concept | vaster |
|------------|---------|--------|
| GDAL / terra / stars | geotransform, grid object | `geo_transform0()`, `dimension`/`extent` |
| odc.geo `GeoBox` | grid spec + boundary | `dimension`/`extent`, `vaster_boundary()` |
| rasterio | rasterize points | `cell_from_xy()` + `tabulate()` |
| ImageMagick | crop geometry string | `magick_geometry()` |

The common thread: these tools bundle grid logic with data, formats, or a CRS.
vaster keeps just the logic, so you can compute cells, coordinates, crops, and
boundaries up front and hand the results to whichever tool does the I/O.
